..
Key Message 1...Mainly dry weather expected through Saturday.

Ridging at the surface and aloft will crest across our area this 
afternoon/evening...then will slide eastward and out across New 
England tonight and Saturday. Meanwhile...a broad upper level trough 
over Ontario and Quebec will extend southward and begin to phase 
with a compact but vigorous shortwave trough making its way across 
the Upper Midwest and Lower Ohio Valley...resulting in a sharpening/ 
deepening upper trough extending all the way from Hudson Bay to the 
Ohio Valley Saturday evening.

For the most part...the departing ridging should maintain enough of 
an influence on our region to keep our area mainly dry through the 
day Saturday. That said...with the eastern edge of the above trough 
beginning to encroach upon our region...can't completely rule out a 
couple isolated showers/storms skirting by our northwestern 
periphery later tonight/Saturday...and then developing along/inland 
from developing lake breeze boundaries over WNY Saturday afternoon 
with diurnal heating and an uptick in humidity levels.

Key Message 2...Showers and thunderstorms develop for Saturday night-
Monday, with locally heavy rainfall again becoming possible.

Latest guidance suite suggests that the sharp/narrow upper level 
trough will continue to slowly push eastward during the second half 
of the weekend into early next week...with the southern end of the 
trough likely breaking off and consolidating into a slow-moving 
closed low somewhere between the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic states 
sometime in the Monday-Tuesday time frame. At the surface...a rather 
wavy cold front will slowly push eastward across southern Ontario 
and then across our region sometime between Sunday and the first 
part of Monday...with another broad surface low then forming 
underneath the closed low early next week. 

Model guidance continues to struggle with the evolution of this 
pattern Sunday through early next week...particularly with respect 
to the timing and placement of the developing cutoff low...in which 
a considerable degree of uncertainty persists. This being said...a 
notable general trend over the last 24 hours is for a slowing of the 
frontal boundary and its eventual passage across/departure from our 
region. With this in mind the attendant next round of unsettled 
weather now is looking more likely to extend into Monday...though 
both faster or slower departures of this remain plausible at this 
point given continued model inconsistencies and the resulting degree 
of forecast uncertainty. 

What still appears more certain is that increasingly unsettled 
conditions will begin Saturday night...then will continue through 
Sunday/Sunday night as the upper trough axis and wavy cold front 
approach...then work into our region. During this time the deep 
south-southwesterly flow out ahead of this system will spread a 
plume of rich Gulf-based moisture across our region...with PWATs 
increasing to near 2 inches. Within this environment...warm 
advection/isentropic ascent will result in increasing probabilities 
for showers and thunderstorms across our area Saturday night and 
Sunday...with this further aided during Sunday by the approach of 
the front/trough axis...increasing low level convergence along the 
nose of a 30-40 knot low level jet...and the development of weak to 
modest diurnally-driven instability. Given the high atmospheric 
moisture content and near-parallel nature of the low-mid level flow 
to the approaching front and trough axis...the potential will exist 
for storms with heavy rainfall to develop and train out ahead 
of/along the approaching frontal boundary Sunday into Sunday 
night...which could in turn pose a risk for localized flash 
flooding. This remains well captured by WPC's Marginal risk for 
excessive rainfall for far western New York for Saturday night...and 
the entire area for Sunday/Sunday night. While a decent amount of 
deep-layer shear (30-40 knots) does look to develop across far WNY 
on Sunday and then linger across our region through Sunday 
night...the presence of only weak to at best modest instability 
currently looks to largely preclude much of an organized severe 
weather threat.  

As mentioned above...with the slower trend to the passage of the 
front/trough axis there now appears to be a decent likelihood that 
at least some showers/storms will linger into Monday as well...and 
with this in mind have upped PoPs for the start of the new work 
week. Depending upon exactly what happens with the evolution of the 
closed low...at least some chance for showers/storms may then linger 
through the middle of next week.
